short: A spectacular diplomatic summit demonstrating England's status as a European power.
full:
From 7 to 24 June 1520, Henry VIII of England and Francis I of France met at Balinghem, near Calais, to celebrate the Treaty of London and cement a personal alliance. The summit was designed to display the immense wealth and cultural sophistication of both Renaissance monarchs. Encampments of temporary palaces, pavilions, and tents were constructed, heavily decorated with the expensive gold-woven fabric that gave the event its name.

Over two weeks, the courts engaged in jousting, archery, wrestling, and banquets, attended by thousands of nobles and retainers. Despite the ruinous expense, the diplomatic achievements were entirely superficial. No substantive agreements were reached, and the displays of mutual affection barely masked an intense personal rivalry between the two kings. Within two years, the ostentatious alliance had collapsed, and England allied with the Holy Roman Emperor Charles V to wage war against France, rendering the summit a magnificent but politically sterile exercise in royal propaganda.
